newsitem.title: INDIA: India's political crisis deepens before test vote.
newsitem.headline: India's political crisis deepens before test vote.

text.p: India's political crisis deepened on Thursday after the rebellious Congress party ordered lawmakers to vote to topple their former ally, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Congress issued a notice to deputies to vote against a confidence motion which Deve Gowda was set to put before the lower house of parliament on Friday.
The party whip order raised pressure on Deve Gowda's centre-left ruling coalition to bow to its rival's demand that the prime minister relinquish power before the vote.

Talks between the two groups ended in deadlock, with the United Front alliance refusing to abandon its support for Deve Gowda, who took power as the head of the minority government last June after inconclusive elections.
"We stand by our demand for change in leadership," said Tariq Anwar, political secretary to Congress president Sitaram Kesri. "The talks have failed."
"Our offer -- that if they change their leader, we are prepared to talk or resume the talks -- still stands," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told reporters.

"If by 11 o'clock tomorrow the matter is not resolved, then we will vote against the government," he said. The lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, was set to convene at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) on Friday to take up the confidence motion.
The vote is tentatively scheduled for 8 p.m. New Delhi time (1430 GMT), the Press Trust of India reported.
Deve Gowda's allies said Congress's reluctance to soften its stance meant the nation would have to hold its second general elections in a year.
"Read my lips. There will be elections. Let the people decide," Laloo Prasad Yadav, Bihar state chief minister and a United Front leader, told reporters.

But Congress held out the prospect of trying to establish a new ruling coalition in talks with the 15-party United Front even if Deve Gowda lost the vote of confidence. A senior United Front official said Congress had sought another round of talks on Thursday evening.

"Even after the government falls, we are prepared to negotiate any arrangement that will contain communal forces," he said, referring to the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which Congress and the United Front accuse of fanning communal tensions by favouring India's Hindu majority.

Politicians said Congress appeared to want Deve Gowda to step down before the test vote while the United Front and Congress sought to find a new leader from either one of the camps, averting snap polls.
If both Congress and the BJP voted against Deve Gowda on Friday, his government would be sure to fall as it lacks an outright majority in the hung parliament.

That would force President Shankar Dayal Sharma to turn to another politician -- probably from either Congress or the BJP -- to try to form a fresh government, or the president could call general elections.

But a senior United Front leader said that if no deal was reached, Deve Gowda would dissolve parliament before facing the test vote. "The United Front will seek the dissolution of parliament before a vote of confidence," he said.
The Press Trust of India said a group of 20 to 30 Congress deputies had asked their party to withdraw the notice to vote against Deve Gowda, apparently marking a split in the party.

The Hindu nationalist BJP, which emerged as parliament's largest party in inconclusive elections last year, controls 193 seats in the 542-member lower house. The 15-member United Front has 180 deputies, while Congress controls 140 votes.
